blocks.text: The Time Based Key Value Store problem asks you to design a data structure that behaves like a map, except every value written to a key is stamped with a timestamp, and every read asks for the value that was true at some point in the past rather than the value that is true right now.

It shows up constantly in interviews because it looks, at first glance, like a hashing exercise. The real skill being tested is noticing that the query it actually asks, find the most recent write at or before a given moment in time, is exactly the classic binary search floor pattern wearing a different costume.

items: set(key, value, timestamp): stores value for key at the given timestamp. Timestamps passed to successive set calls on the same key are guaranteed to always increase strictly.
get(key, timestamp): returns the value that was set for key at the largest timestamp that is less than or equal to the given timestamp, or an empty string if no such timestamp exists.

blocks.text: set(key, value, timestamp) is the simpler of the two operations. It records that, at this exact moment in time, this key took on this value. There is no requirement to overwrite, merge, or reconcile anything, every call is a brand new entry in that key's history. The strictly increasing timestamp guarantee is handed to you by the problem statement, it is not something your implementation needs to check or enforce, but it is the single fact that makes everything else in this problem tractable.

get(key, timestamp) is where the actual difficulty lives. Read the wording carefully, it asks for the value at the largest stored timestamp that is less than or equal to the query timestamp. It is not asking for the closest timestamp, and it is not asking for an exact match. A query for timestamp 100 when the only recorded timestamps are 1 and 4 should still return the value written at timestamp 4, because 4 is the largest timestamp that does not exceed 100.

Everything in this problem hinges on one guarantee: timestamps supplied to set for the same key always increase strictly. That guarantee is what allows every later step, from the data structure choice to the binary search, to be correct.

items: If key has never been passed to set at all, get must return an empty string.
If key exists but every stored timestamp for it is greater than the query timestamp, get must also return an empty string, since no valid floor exists.

content.title: 2. Why This Is a Find the Floor Problem in Disguise

blocks.text: In classic binary search terminology, the floor (sometimes called the predecessor) of a target value inside a sorted sequence is the largest element in that sequence that is still less than or equal to the target. Finding a floor is one of the oldest binary search variants there is, and it generalizes the plain exact match search that most people learn first.

Now look again at what happens on the set side of this problem. Because timestamps for a single key are guaranteed to arrive in strictly increasing order, the sequence of (timestamp, value) pairs recorded for that key is sorted by timestamp the instant it is written. There is never a need to insert into the middle of that sequence, and there is never an out of order write to reconcile. Sortedness is not something we have to build, it falls out of the problem's own guarantee for free.

Once that is understood, get(key, timestamp) stops looking like a custom lookup and becomes a direct restatement of the textbook floor query: given a sorted sequence of timestamps for this key, find the rightmost entry whose timestamp does not exceed the query timestamp. That is the entire problem. Everything from here on is just implementing a correct and efficient floor search.

The trick in this problem is not algorithmic, it is a framing trick. The moment you recognize get as a floor query on an already sorted sequence, the implementation becomes mechanical: pick a data structure that keeps each key's history sorted for free, then binary search it.

content.title: 3. The Design: A Hash Map of Sorted Vectors

blocks.text: The natural design follows directly from the framing above. Use a hash map from key to a vector of (timestamp, value) pairs, one vector per key, holding that key's entire write history in the order it was written.

Because the timestamp guarantee promises strict increase for every set call on a given key, simply calling push_back at the end of that key's vector keeps the vector sorted by timestamp at all times. No separate sorting step is ever needed, no insertion in the middle of the vector is ever needed, and no re balancing of any kind is required. The data arrives sorted, so the structure that stores it stays sorted automatically.

blocks.caption: Each key maps to its own vector of (timestamp, value) pairs, already sorted by construction.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865013-805398483.png
blocks.alt: The Design: A Hash Map of Sorted Vectors

blocks.text: It is worth contrasting this with a heavier design, such as giving each key a balanced ordered map or a tree structure. That would still be correct, but it would be strictly worse here: those structures pay for the ability to insert out of order and stay balanced, a cost this problem never asks you to pay, since every insertion for a key is already guaranteed to land at the very end of that key's sorted history. A plain vector gets the same sorted guarantee for a fraction of the constant factor and code complexity.

content.title: 4. Worked Trace: Walking Through a Sequence of Calls

blocks.text: Trace the following sequence of calls on a single key, "foo", to see the design in action from an empty store all the way through several queries, including one that has no valid answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Vector for foo after this call","Result","Explanation"],"rows":[["set(\"foo\",\"bar1\",1)","[(1,bar1)]","void","First write for this key. A single element vector is trivially sorted."],["get(\"foo\",1)","[(1,bar1)]","\"bar1\"","Exact match at timestamp 1."],["get(\"foo\",2)","[(1,bar1)]","\"bar1\"","No entry at timestamp 2, so the floor is the largest stored timestamp not exceeding 2, which is 1."],["set(\"foo\",\"bar2\",4)","[(1,bar1),(4,bar2)]","void","Appended at the end. 4 is greater than 1, so the vector stays sorted with no extra work."],["get(\"foo\",4)","[(1,bar1),(4,bar2)]","\"bar2\"","Exact match at timestamp 4."],["get(\"foo\",5)","[(1,bar1),(4,bar2)]","\"bar2\"","No entry at timestamp 5, floor is 4."],["get(\"foo\",0)","[(1,bar1),(4,bar2)]","\"\"","Even the smallest stored timestamp, 1, exceeds 0. No valid floor exists."]]}

blocks.text: Three of these get calls are worth walking through bound by bound, since they cover the three shapes a floor search can take: an exact match found immediately, a floor that requires narrowing the search window, and the case where no floor exists at all.

get("foo", 2) against the single element vector [(1,bar1)]: start with low = 0, high = 0. The midpoint is index 0, whose timestamp is 1. Since 1 is less than or equal to 2, this index is a candidate floor, so it is recorded and the search moves right by setting low = 1. Now low exceeds high, so the loop stops with the last recorded candidate, index 0, as the answer, giving "bar1".

get("foo", 5) against the two element vector [(1,bar1),(4,bar2)]: start with low = 0, high = 1. The midpoint is index 0, timestamp 1, which is less than or equal to 5, so it is recorded as a candidate and the search moves right with low = 1. Now low = 1, high = 1, midpoint is index 1, timestamp 4, also less than or equal to 5, so it replaces the candidate and the search again moves right with low = 2. Since low now exceeds high, the loop stops and the last recorded candidate, index 1, is the answer, giving "bar2".

get("foo", 0) against the same vector [(1,bar1),(4,bar2)]: start with low = 0, high = 1. The midpoint is index 0, timestamp 1, which is not less than or equal to 0, so this index cannot be a candidate and the search moves left with high = -1. Since low now exceeds high, the loop stops with no candidate ever recorded, so the function returns an empty string.

blocks.caption: Binary search narrowing to the floor for get("foo", 5): the window shrinks until the largest timestamp not exceeding 5 is found.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865013-587028463.png
blocks.alt: Worked Trace: Walking Through a Sequence of Calls

blocks.text: A linear scan would also produce a correct answer here. Walking a key's vector from the end backward and stopping at the first entry whose timestamp is less than or equal to the query timestamp finds exactly the same floor that binary search finds, since the vector is sorted.

The reason a linear scan is still worth mentioning, and still worth ruling out, is that it is correct for the same underlying reason binary search is correct, namely the guaranteed sortedness of each key's history, yet it fails to make use of that structure efficiently. Its cost is proportional to how many timestamps that specific key has accumulated, which for a frequently written key can grow arbitrarily large over the lifetime of the store. A linear scan degrades to O(n) work per query exactly when it matters most, on hot keys with long histories.

Binary search is only valid to reach for at all because the vector is guaranteed sorted by construction. Binary search is unsound on unsorted data, full stop, it can silently return a wrong answer if the invariant it depends on does not actually hold. The strictly increasing timestamp guarantee from the problem statement is precisely what licenses using binary search here. Without that guarantee, a linear scan or an explicit sort before every query would be the only correct option.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time per get()","Correctness","When it matters"],"rows":[["Linear scan from the end","O(n)","Correct","Fine for keys with only a handful of writes, degrades badly on keys written to constantly"],["Binary search on the sorted vector","O(log n)","Correct","Relies on the strictly increasing guarantee, scales cleanly even for keys with very long histories"]]}

blocks.text: The chain of reasoning is short and worth memorizing: strictly increasing timestamps guarantee a sorted sequence per key, a sorted sequence licenses binary search, and binary search turns an O(n) floor lookup into an O(log n) one.

There are two equally valid ways to implement the floor search in C++: a hand rolled binary search loop that tracks the best candidate seen so far, or a call to the standard library's upper_bound with a small index adjustment afterward. Both are shown below.
Custom binary search loop

The key idea in this loop is floorIdx: it always holds the best candidate found so far, and every time the midpoint's timestamp qualifies (it is less than or equal to the target), the search keeps pushing right to see if an even later valid timestamp exists, rather than stopping immediately. If the midpoint's timestamp is too large, the search only moves left, it never touches floorIdx. When the loop ends, floorIdx is either the correct answer or still -1, meaning no floor exists.
Using upper_bound

The standard library alternative uses upper_bound, but it requires care around one specific off by one subtlety. upper_bound returns an iterator to the first element that is strictly greater than the target, not the floor itself. The floor, if it exists, sits one position before that iterator. This means after calling upper_bound, the code must step the returned iterator back by one to reach the actual floor, and critically, it must first check that the returned iterator is not already at the very beginning of the vector, because stepping a begin iterator backward is undefined behavior and also signals that no valid floor exists at all.

set is O(1) amortized. It only ever appends to the end of the vector belonging to that key, and push_back on a vector is O(1) amortized thanks to geometric capacity growth, occasional reallocations are spread out over many calls so the average cost per call stays constant.

get is O(log n), where n is the number of timestamps stored for that specific key, not the total size of the store. A key with a long write history costs more per query than a key with only a few writes, which is exactly what a binary search over that key's own vector should cost.

Space is O(m), where m is the total number of set calls across every key combined, since every single call appends exactly one (timestamp, value) pair somewhere and nothing is ever discarded or compacted.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Time complexity","Explanation"],"rows":[["set","O(1) amortized","Append only, no search or shifting required"],["get","O(log n) per key","Binary search over that key's sorted vector, n is that key's write count"],["Overall space","O(m) total","m is the total number of set calls made across all keys"]]}

items: Using a linear scan instead of binary search. It is correct but performs poorly on keys with long write histories, and it fails to demonstrate the technique the problem is actually testing.

Off by one errors converting an upper_bound result into a floor. Forgetting that upper_bound points one position past the floor, and forgetting to check the result is not already at the beginning of the vector before stepping it back.
Assuming get wants the closest timestamp. It does not. A query timestamp of 100 with only timestamps 1 and 4 recorded must still return the value at 4, not treat 100 as out of range.

Forgetting the empty string case entirely. Both an unknown key and a query timestamp earlier than every recorded timestamp for a known key must return an empty string, these are two different situations that both lead to the same result.

Re sorting on every get. Since the vector is already sorted by construction thanks to the strictly increasing timestamp guarantee, sorting again before each query wastes an entire O(n log n) pass for nothing.

blocks.text: Nearly every mistake on this list traces back to forgetting, or not fully trusting, the strictly increasing timestamp guarantee. Once that guarantee is taken at face value, the sorted vector design and the binary search that rides on top of it fall out with very little room for error.

items: Medium Time Based Key Value Store (LC 981): the canonical version of this exact problem.

The same floor and predecessor binary search technique generalizes far beyond this one problem, to any situation phrased as "find the most recent event at or before time X" over a per key or per entity sorted history.

blocks.text: That generalization shows up under different names across systems style interview questions too: retrieving the most recent price of a stock as of a given moment, looking up the version of a document that was active at a given commit time, or finding the last known state of a cache entry before an invalidation. In every one of these, the underlying shape is identical to this problem, a sorted per key sequence and a floor query against it.

items: Can you state precisely what get(key, timestamp) returns when there is no exact timestamp match?
Do you see why the strictly increasing timestamp guarantee means each key's history is sorted without ever calling sort?
Can you explain why get() is a floor, or predecessor, query rather than a nearest or exact match query?
Can you implement the binary search floor loop from scratch, including the case where no floor exists?
If using upper_bound, can you explain exactly why the result must be stepped back by one, and why that step must be guarded against the beginning of the vector?
Can you state the time complexity of set and get in terms of a specific key's write count, not the total size of the store?

blocks.text: Walking through this checklist out loud is usually enough to signal to an interviewer that the floor search framing was understood from the start, rather than arrived at by trial and error.
